To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the symmetric complete graph can dominate the star in terms of total welfare; (2) a dominating symmetric network does not need to be stable; (3) the star and the complete network can be dominated by a small world; and, (4) the star and complete network can be stable and not dominate any other network.

(i) decreasing returns to investment in link strength can make the symmetric complete network more desirable than a star; and (ii) decreasing returns can also make small-world networks more attractive than the star or the symmetric complete network.
(a) the complete network can be a stable equilibrium when the link strength is concave; (b) the star network can be a Nash equilibrium even when the link strength function is concave.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of networks with endogenous link strength and decreasing returns to investment, and we show that the resulting equilibrium network can be quite complex.
the formation of a network with decreasing returns to investment in links.
the role of the strength technology in the formation of networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the star and the complete network do not necessarily dominate all other network structures in terms of total network utility.
the star network is no longer the most efficient network architecture.
the star and complete networks are less robust in the concave case than in the convex case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, the strength technology matters in network formation.
the strength technology is not only a key determinant for the structure of a stable network, but also a crucial factor for the network to be dominated by a complete network.
the star network is the most likely to be stable when the strength technology exhibits decreasing returns to investment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the strength of links between agents is a crucial determinant of network formation.
network formation with decreasing returns to investment is a more general framework for the analysis of networks.

the strength of direct links can be a decreasing function of the investment in each link, and the resulting equilibrium network structures can be quite different from those in existing models of network investment.
